scenario: AITA for visiting my son unannounced. | My son’s(19) in an university. He’s in a different city and lives in an apartment with 2 of his friends. Ever since he left(2 months ago) he just started ignoring me. I didn’t call him excessively, maybe once in two days. He’d hang up or not answer and text me later that he’s busy. Few days ago I was in the city for unrelated reason. I called him because I wanted to visit him but he didn’t answer so I just went to the apartment. His friend answered the door, my son was sleeping. The apartment was filthy, empty bottles everywhere, 5 or more ashtrays filled with cigarette butts. Dirty dishes to the roof. My son woke up and he was surprised when he saw me. He told me that I should’ve called him or something. We talked for a bit and he seemed kinda annoyed. I joked about the place needing a good clean and he just rolled his eyes. I asked him why he was ignoring me. He said that he’s just busy with studying and all that stuff and I should give him space when he needs it. He also said that it was weird that I just showed up unannounced.

prediction.raw: I would say 1 (You Are The Asshole) in this scenario. As a parent, it's natural to want to visit and check in on your child, especially if you feel like you're being ignored. However, showing up unannounced at your son's apartment, where he lives with friends, can be seen as an overstep of boundaries. Your son is 19, which means he's an adult and likely values his independence. By not answering your calls or responding with brief texts, he's indicating that he needs space and time to focus on his studies and his own life. Ignoring you might not be the most respectful way to handle the situation, but it's possible that he's feeling overwhelmed or struggling to balance his responsibilities. By showing up unannounced, you're not respecting his boundaries or giving him the space he's asking for. It's also possible that your visit, although well-intentioned, might be perceived as an attempt to exert control or monitor his behavior, which could be seen as intrusive or embarrassing, especially in front of his friends. It's great that you're concerned about your son's well-being, but it's essential to respect his autonomy and communicate with him in a way that works for both of you. Perhaps you could try having an open and honest conversation with him about your concerns and feelings, and work together to find a compromise that respects his need for independence while also addressing your desire to stay connected.
